help.main:
ccdt: use the original Claude Code on a CC Desk Tunnel server from your own terminal, sharing sessions with the desktop client.

Usage:
  ccdt                   Continue this directory’s project’s latest session; start one if there is none
  ccdt -r                Pick one of this project’s sessions to open (add --all to pick from every session)
  ccdt new [title]       Start a session in this directory
  ccdt sessions [--all]  List this project’s sessions; --all lists every session; --json prints JSON
  ccdt online            Keep this computer online without a terminal, so Claude can run commands here;
                         reconnects on its own, Ctrl+C ends it. Can run in the background on a headless server
  ccdt usage             Subscription quota and usage figures
  ccdt config            View and change settings: pick each with the arrow keys in the terminal
  ccdt config name [val] View or change one setting, for scripts; the value default restores the default
  ccdt server            Servers signed in to: pick the one to connect to by default, or sign in to another
  ccdt login [wss URL]   Sign in to a server; without a URL, pick one saved by the desktop client. --fingerprint
                         certificate fingerprint, --token-stdin reads the token from standard input, --no-save keeps nothing
  ccdt logout            Sign out of a server (pick one when signed in to several); the others stay
  ccdt open <session ID> Open by ID (the first few characters will do), for scripts
  ccdt upgrade [--yes]   Upgrade the server (asks first; --yes doesn’t), then switch ccdt to the server’s version;
                         says so when sessions are running, and you can choose to force it (--force doesn’t ask)
  ccdt upgrade --check   Only check for a new version
  ccdt --version         The version, which must match the server’s

For programs and other agents (written like claude -p; see ccdt help agents):
  ccdt -p "task"         Start a session in this directory’s project, send the task, print Claude’s reply when the turn ends
                         -c continues the latest session, -r <session> a given one, --bg returns once sent
  ccdt status <session>  What it’s doing, what it’s waiting for
  ccdt tell <session> "…"  Add an instruction: while running, it joins the turn under way
  ccdt wait <session>    Wait until the turn ends, or Claude waits for an approval or an answer
  ccdt approve|deny <session>  Approve or deny what Claude is waiting on, then wait until it stops again; ccdt answer <session> "answer" answers a question
  ccdt logs <session>    Recent messages and tool calls
  ccdt stop <session>    Stop the turn under way
  ccdt acp               Run as an ACP (Agent Client Protocol) agent, for Zed, JetBrains, acpx and others

Options:
  -s                     Pick the server first, then do the rest, as in ccdt -s -r
  --server <name>        Name the server: a connection name from the desktop client, a host name or a URL; enough to tell it apart
Without either, ccdt connects to the server it connected to last.

Use it like a local claude: it runs as long as the window is open and reconnects after a dropped network; quitting Claude Code or closing the window ends it.
help.agents:
ccdt for programs and other agents: hand a task to Claude Code on the server and follow it until it’s done.
The session is the same one the desktop client shows: its window shows what it’s doing, and you can step in and approve there too.

Dispatch (written like claude -p):
  ccdt -p "task" [options]
    By default starts a session in this directory’s project; -c continues this project’s latest session; -r <session> a given one
    --bg                    Return the session ID once sent, without waiting for the result
    --output-format text|json|stream-json   text by default: only Claude’s last reply;
                            stream-json prints text, thinking, tool calls and results, and status, line by line
    --permission-mode auto|default|plan|acceptEdits|bypassPermissions
    --model <model>  --effort low|medium|high|xhigh|max  --title <title>
    --timeout <seconds>     Wait at most this long; if still running then, return (exit code 6)
  The task can come from standard input too: echo "task" | ccdt -p

Follow up (<session> is the session ID; the first few characters will do):
  ccdt status <session> [--json]     What it’s doing, what it’s waiting for
  ccdt wait <session> [--timeout seconds] [--output-format …]   Wait until the turn ends or needs a person
  ccdt tell <session> "more"          Add an instruction; while Claude is working it joins this turn, to correct course
  ccdt approve <session> [--mode auto|acceptEdits|default]   Approve the request; --mode is for plans only
  ccdt deny <session> ["feedback"]    Deny; for a plan, the feedback says how to change it
  ccdt answer <session> "answer 1" ["answer 2" …]   Answer Claude’s questions in order; separate multiple choices with commas
  ccdt logs <session> [--last N] [--json]   The last N (default 20) messages and tool calls
  ccdt stop <session>                Stop this turn
  ccdt sessions [--all] --json       List sessions

ACP: editors and agents that speak the Agent Client Protocol (Zed, JetBrains, acpx and others) set ccdt acp as the agent command;
the session goes in the project of the directory it’s started in.

Exit codes: 0 done (or sent with --bg); 2 waiting for an approval or an answer; 3 failed; 4 stopped; 5 can’t connect or not signed in;
6 still running at --timeout; 1 any other error. The result goes to standard output; what happened and what to do next to standard error.

json result: {"session_id","state","result","is_error","approval"?}. state is completed, background (the turn ended
and background tasks are still running; Claude carries on when they finish), awaiting_approval, awaiting_answer, failed, cancelled
or running. approval says what it’s waiting for: {"kind":"tool","tool","input","reason"?}, {"kind":"plan","plan"}
or {"kind":"question","questions":[{"question","options","multiSelect"}]}.

Approvals: when Claude asks for approval or asks a question, ccdt -p and ccdt wait stop and leave it to the caller to approve, deny or answer.
After replying, those three commands wait on like ccdt -p, print the result and exit with the same codes, providing this computer’s
execution channel while they wait; with --bg they only reply (later commands that run on this computer then need the desktop client or ccdt online open).
The desktop client can answer at the same time; whichever answers first counts. To be asked less, dispatch with --permission-mode.

Tips:
- For a long task, run ccdt -p inside your own background task and you’ll know when it ends; or send it with --bg and ccdt wait later.
- Which computer Claude runs commands on: the session’s, and a new session’s is the one running ccdt.
  ccdt -p provides this computer’s execution channel while it waits; after --bg, keep the desktop client or ccdt online open.
